title: Convolution with a box window
context: Convolution; equation eq-convol-1d.
notes: The shaded interval is [x-epsilon,x+epsilon], the support of g(x-t), with g the unnormalized box on [-epsilon,epsilon]. The dashed red curve is the exact sliding integral of the same displayed signal, computed by integrating its affine and sinusoidal terms; the red dot is at (x,(f*g)(x)). The illustrated width is 2 epsilon=1.5, so the convolution is an integral, not a unit-mass average. The curve and shaded area use the same normalization.

title: Convolution becomes multiplication
context: Convolution theorem; equation eq-convol-fourier.
notes: The diagram uses the chapter convention F(f*g)=f-hat times g-hat. Both vertical arrows apply the Fourier transform, making the square commute; the original reverse Fourier arrow is equivalently written in the forward direction.

title: Cardinal splines by convolution
context: Convolution; Figure fig-splines.
notes: The box, triangle, and quadratic spline are exact centered cardinal B-splines B0, B1=B0*B0, and B2=B1*B0. The original final handwritten symbol is unclear; explicit degree and convolution labels replace it.

title: Translation equivariance
context: Translation-invariant operators; T_tau f(x)=f(x-tau).
notes: The original square is made explicit with T_tau f=f(.-tau). The bottom-right value is H(T_tau f)=T_tau(Hf); this is equivariance, called translation invariance in the chapter.

title: Fourier modes align at the Dirac comb
context: Poisson formula and distributions; finite Dirichlet kernel.
notes: Three real Fourier modes cos(n omega), n=1,2,3, are shown. They all equal one at multiples of 2pi. The distributional comb identity is stated separately; a finite sum is not drawn as literal Dirac masses.

title: One radix-two FFT step
context: Discrete Fourier transform; recursion immediately before Figure fig-fft.
notes: Four distinct arrows connect both input halves to both the sum and difference. The difference is multiplied componentwise by the twiddle-factor vector before its half-size FFT. On the right, individual arrows map the two output streams into alternating even and odd positions; the first three entries are shown for N>=8. The zero-based indices match the DFT and the interleaving definition in the chapter. Crossings are not connections.

title: Spatial zero padding refines frequency sampling
context: Fourier approximation via spatial zero padding; Figure fig-padding-spacial.
notes: An exact analytic example uses N=12, Q=24 and f(x)=sin squared(pi x) on [0,1], zero elsewhere. The Q spatial samples stop at T-1/N, where T=Q/N; the final point T is excluded. The continuous curve is the magnitude of the actual Fourier transform, and the Q markers are normalized DFT magnitudes at signed indices -Q/2 through Q/2-1. Thus the unchanged Nyquist bound is pi N and the frequency step is 2pi/T, correcting the handwritten reciprocal bounds. The DFT approximates the continuous transform by a Riemann sum; it does not equal it exactly. These are analytic values, not measurements.

title: Spectral zero padding interpolates the samples
context: Fourier interpolation via spectral zero padding; Figure fig-padding-fourier.
notes: The retained signed-frequency coefficients are padded with zeros, and the inverse transform is multiplied by Q/N. The illustrative trigonometric polynomial and coefficient magnitudes are consistent for N=5 and Q=15; dark markers identify the five original samples and smaller colored markers the finer grid. These are analytic example values, not measurements. Odd N avoids the even-length Nyquist splitting convention.

title: A plane wave and its normal direction
context: Fourier in multiple dimensions; tensor products of complex exponentials.
notes: The parallel lines are constant-phase sets, normal to the wave vector omega. The marked point lies on the emphasized phase line, and the right-angle marker joins that line to its normal. This indicates geometry rather than a propagation direction. Integer wave vectors apply on the periodic domain; the general figure uses omega in R squared.

title: A square with opposite edges identified
context: Multidimensional torus; (R / 2pi Z) squared.
notes: Opposite sides of the square carry matching oriented arrows. Identifying each pair produces the two-dimensional torus. The pictured doughnut is a topological visualization, not an isometric embedding of the flat quotient.

title: A periodic two-dimensional grid
context: Discrete multidimensional Fourier basis; product of cyclic index sets.
notes: A four-by-four representative grid illustrates the two periodic coordinate directions. A step beyond the last displayed index wraps back to zero; the first and last displayed vertices remain distinct. The identifications occur after N1 or N2 steps, so the rectangle has no physical boundary. The grid size is illustrative.

title: Heat diffusion is Gaussian convolution
context: Fourier multipliers and differential equations; Figure fig-heat.
notes: The left curves show an illustrative signal with two Fourier modes at time zero and after positive diffusion times. The right curves are Gaussian heat kernels for the same two times: increasing time broadens the kernel and lowers its peak. The normalization and variance follow the chapter heat equation.

title: Continuum and discrete Laplacian spectra
context: Finite domain and discretization; equations eq-disc-diff-2 and eq-fft-lapl.
notes: The original positive curves are explicitly labeled as negative eigenvalues divided by N squared. The continuum curve is (2pi k/N) squared, reaching pi squared at Nyquist; the discrete curve is 4 sin squared(pi k/N), reaching four. Actual Laplacian eigenvalues are nonpositive.

title: A small geodesic ball on a surface
context: Laplace--Beltrami operator and the small-ball mean-value expansion.
notes: The sketch is a local surface patch containing a geodesic ball centered at x. The ellipse represents the projected ball, not a claim that geodesic balls are Euclidean circles. The displayed expansion retains the necessary epsilon-squared scaling and dimension-dependent constant.

title: Colatitude and azimuth on the sphere
context: Spherical harmonics; x=(sin theta cos phi,sin theta sin phi,cos theta).
notes: Theta is colatitude from the positive north axis, matching the chapter formula; the original angle is ambiguous and may instead suggest latitude. Phi is equatorial azimuth. The point, its equatorial projection, both angle arcs, the equator and the poles are projected from one consistent unit sphere. A viewing elevation of 30 degrees separates the arcs. Screen angles need not equal spatial angles, and the projected poles lie inside the circular silhouette. The illustrative point has colatitude 50 degrees and azimuth 38 degrees.

title: A weighted graph and its local Laplacian
context: Graph Laplacian; Delta=W-D.
notes: The graph patch preserves the intended local adjacency picture, highlighting an edge between vertices i and j with weight w_ij. Unreadable numerical marks are not assigned values. The Laplacian sign matches the chapter nonpositive convention.

title: Orthogonalizing a cardinal spline
context: Spectral orthogonalization; Proposition prop-spectral-ortho and Figure fig-spline-ortho.
notes: The formula identifies the handwritten example as the orthogonal linear spline. Its triangular generator has compact support, while the orthogonalized function has alternating exponentially decaying tails. The replacement uses the correct Fourier multiplier sqrt(3/(2+cos omega)); its cosine coefficients were evaluated by 8192-point midpoint quadrature. Axis ticks distinguish the generator interval [-1,1] from the displayed orthogonalized interval [-4,4], which uses a compressed horizontal scale. Four small degree examples recover the original spline-family sketches.

title: Sharp and smooth frequency partitions
context: Multiresolution detail spaces; Figure fig-spline-vs-shannon.
notes: The Shannon row shows the exact low-pass band |omega|<=pi and the next two dyadic wavelet bands. The spline row deliberately shows schematic smooth overlap, not the spectrum of a named spline order. Only a finite frequency window is drawn; the partition identity refers to all scales. Cropped neighboring prose in the scan is omitted. The energy of a scale-j wavelet is multiplied by 2 to the power -j to remove its L2 dilation factor, as the displayed identity explains; this gives the factor two on the outer scale-minus-one band.

title: Wrapping a function around the unit interval
context: On bounded domains; f-periodic is the sum of integer translates.
notes: The illustrative compact bump is cos squared(2pi(x-0.87)) for |x-0.87|<=0.25, zero elsewhere. On [0,1], only f(x) and its left-shifted copy f(x+1) contribute, so the drawn sum and matching endpoint values are exact. The profile is not presented as a particular orthogonal wavelet; periodization applies to each basis function individually. No unknown profile or empirical values are inferred from the scan.

title: One representative of each periodic translate
context: On bounded domains; 0<=n<2^{-j}.
notes: The selected translation centers lie in the half-open unit interval. The example j=-2 has four distinct centers; the center at one is the same periodic translate as zero. Smooth pulse profiles are schematic and do not assert that this particular shape generates an orthogonal wavelet basis.

title: Haar filter coefficients from overlap integrals
context: Discrete wavelet transform; equation eq-dfn-h-g.
notes: The original inner products are +1 for the scaling function and +1 or -1 for the wavelet. The chapter filter definition adds a factor 1/sqrt(2); the resulting h=(1,1)/sqrt(2) and g=(1,-1)/sqrt(2) are therefore explicitly distinguished from the raw overlap integrals.

title: Complementary low-pass and high-pass energies
context: Wavelet design; low-pass and QMF constraints.
notes: The solid and dashed curves are the exact Haar examples |h-hat| squared=2 cos squared(omega/2) and its pi shift=2 sin squared(omega/2). Their sum is two, and the shifted energy equals that of the QMF high-pass filter. The nearby cropped text in the scan is replaced by the complete relevant equality.

title: Vanishing moments and flat filter zeros
context: Wavelet design; vanishing-moment condition eq-cond-vm-fourier.
notes: The drawing separates the low-pass zero at pi from the high-pass zero at zero, avoiding the ambiguous overlaid labels in the scan. The curves are magnitudes for a two-moment QMF example; the derivative statement concerns the smooth filter symbols themselves, including their phases. The displayed zeros have order two, while the formula states the general p-moment equivalence.
